newsitem.title: USA: Chiron sees IL-2 benfits to HIV patients.
newsitem.headline: Chiron sees IL-2 benfits to HIV patients.

text.p: Chiron Corp said Monday a National Institutes of Health study showed outpatient subcutaneous administration of recombinant interleukin (IL-2) in people infected with HIV can produce "substantial and sustained" increases in CD4 cells levels.
Chiron said the results, reported in the April issue of the Journal of Infectious Diseases, support the findings of another NIH study reported in October.

"With these data, we have made significant progress in finding a tolerable outpatient dosing regimen that will achieve considerable, long-term increases in patients' CD4 immune cell levels that have not been realized with antiretroviral therapy alone," said Dr Peter Curtin, associate director of clinical development for Chiron Technologies.

Results from the latest study also indicate that subcutaneous administration of IL-2 provided on an outpatient basis resulted in "noticeably less toxicity" compared to continuous infusion regimens, Chiron said.

"We are collaborating with the NIH to support a Phase III clinical trial using this subcutaneous outpatient regime in a larger patient group. I am convinced that future studies will confirm that IL-2 is safe and effective immunotherapy for the treatment of patients with HIV," said Magnus Lundberg, president of Chiron therapeutics.
In the latest study, 18 HIV-infected patients received a maximum tolerated dose of 15 MIU of IL-2 therapy daily via subcutaneous injection in combination with standard antiviral therapy.
After 12 months, eight patients, or 44 percent, showed a rise in CD4 cell levels of more than 200 cells per cubic millimeter (mm3) from baseline.
Six patients, or 33 percent, experienced an increase of 0-200 cells/mm3, and four patients, or 22 percent, experienced a gradual decline in CD4 cell counts.

The company said that in an extended follow-up of eight patients continuing outpatient IL-2 therapy for nearly three years, five people have maintained CD4 cells counts in the range of 800-2000 cells/mm3, and three patients have sustained counts in the range of 400-600 cells/mm3.

The likelihood and magnitude of increases in CD4 cell levels correlated directly with patients' baseline cell counts; patients with higher CD4 cell counts at baseline had greater positive response to immunotherapy, Chiron said.
Overall, there was no significant increase in HIV RNA plasma (viral load) or p24 antigen levels from baseline in this patient group.

Adverse effects associated with subcutaneous administration of IL-2 were similar in nature, although considerably lower in severity and duration, to those associated with continuous infusion of IL-2. These mild to moderate constitutional effects included fever, fatigue and associated symptoms that were not treatment-limiting.
Chiron said it supplied the recombinant IL-2 used in the study. It markets IL-2 under the trade name Proleukin (aldesleukin) for injection for the treatment of metastatic renal cell cancer.

The company is supporting additional trials in people with HIV infection, with IL-2 and bDNA assays being conducted with U.S. and French cooperative AIDS trial groups and other investigators in the U.S. and abroad.
